claim: Tll is identified as a lamina progenitor cell (LPC) marker, expressed complementary to Elav.
source: Tll is identified as a lamina progenitor cell (LPC) marker, expressed complementary to Elav
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-A''' demonstrating complementary expression patterns of Tll and Elav, and by text description of the experimental observation.

claim: Dac labels both Tll+ LPCs and Elav+ neurons.
source: Dac labels both Tll+ LPCs and Elav+ neurons
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-A''' demonstrating co-expression patterns.

claim: Tll+ cells are localized both within the lamina columns and before the columns.
source: Tll+ cells are localized both within the lamina columns and before the columns
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B-B''' with lamina columns outlined by photoreceptor axons labeled by Chaoptin.

claim: Bsh is expressed in Tll+ Elav- LPCs as well as in Elav+ L4 and L5 neurons.
source: Bsh is expressed in Tll+ Elav LPCs (white dash circle) as well as in Elav+ L4 and L5 neurons
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C-C''' demonstrating Bsh expression patterns in different cell types.

claim: Ap is expressed in L4 neurons.
source: Ap is expressed in L4 neurons
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-D''' demonstrating Ap expression in L4 neurons.

claim: Newborn L4 neurons are Bsh+ Elav+ Ap-.
source: Newborn L4 neurons are Bsh+ Elav+ Ap- (yellow line circle)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-D''' demonstrating marker expression in newborn L4 neurons.

claim: Older L4 neurons are Bsh+ Elav+ Ap+.
source: older L4 neurons are Bsh+ Elav+ Ap+ (white line circle)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-D''' demonstrating marker expression in older L4 neurons.

claim: Pdm3 is expressed in L5 neurons.
source: Pdm3 is expressed in L5 neurons
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-E''' demonstrating Pdm3 expression in L5 neurons.

claim: Newborn L5 neurons are Bsh+ Pdm3-.
source: Newborn L5 neurons are Bsh+ Pdm3- (yellow line circle)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-E''' demonstrating marker expression in newborn L5 neurons.

claim: Older L5 neurons are Bsh+ Pdm3+.
source: older L5 neurons are Bsh+ Pdm3+ (white line circle)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-E''' demonstrating marker expression in older L5 neurons.

claim: Bsh, Ap, and Pdm3 expressions are maintained in adults.
source: Bsh, Ap, and Pdm3 expressions are maintained in adults
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F-F'' demonstrating continued expression of these markers in adult flies.

claim: Bsh was first detected in a subset of Tll+ LPCs.
source: we found that Bsh was first detected in a subset of Tll+ LPCs (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating Bsh expression in LPCs.

claim: Ap and Pdm3 were first detected much later in L4 and L5 neurons, respectively.
source: In contrast, Ap and Pdm3 were first detected much later in L4 and L5 neurons, respectively (Figure 1D–E)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-E demonstrating temporal expression patterns.

claim: Ap and Pdm3 were never detected in LPCs or newborn L4 or L5 neurons.
source: Ap and Pdm3 were never detected in LPCs or newborn L4 or L5 neurons (Figure 1D–E)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D-E demonstrating absence of expression in early developmental stages.

claim: Bsh is expressed prior to Ap and Pdm3.
source: showing that Bsh is expressed prior to Ap and Pdm3
evidence: Inferred from temporal expression data showing Bsh in LPCs while Ap and Pdm3 appear later in neurons.

claim: Bsh expression is initiated in LPCs, while Ap and Pdm3 are initiated in neurons.
source: We conclude that Bsh expression is initiated in LPCs, while Ap and Pdm3 are initiated in neurons
evidence: Supported by temporal and spatial expression data from Figure 1.

claim: Bsh is referred to as a primary HDTF due to its earlier expression.
source: Due to its earlier expression, we refer to Bsh as a primary HDTF
evidence: Based on temporal expression data showing Bsh appears before Ap and Pdm3.

claim: Ap and Pdm3 are referred to as secondary HDTFs due to their later expression.
source: due to their later expression, we refer to Ap and Pdm3 as secondary HDTFs (Figure 1H)
evidence: Based on temporal expression data showing Ap and Pdm3 appear after Bsh.

claim: R27G05-Gal4 is turned on in LPCs.
source: To confirm whether R27G05-Gal4 is turned on in LPCs, we used R27G05-Gal4>UAS-myristoylated-GFP, and indeed, GFP can be detected in all LPCs and lamina neurons until ~66 hr after pupa formation (APF) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, D, E)
evidence: Supported by GFP expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, D, E.

claim: R27G05-Gal4 can be turned on in lamina neurons.
source: To test whether R27G05-Gal4 can be turned on in lamina neurons, we took advantage of tubP-Gal80[ts] to temporally control R27G05-Gal4>UAS-myristoylated-GFP. We found that GFP can be detected in most lamina neurons when tubP-Gal80[ts] was inactivated from the beginning of lamina neurogenesis
evidence: Supported by temporal control experiments using Gal80ts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: GFP is absent in most lamina neurons when tubP-Gal80[ts] was inactivated from the end of lamina neurogenesis.
source: In contrast, GFP is absent in most lamina neurons when tubP-Gal80[ts] was inactivated from the end of lamina neurogenesis, suggesting that R27G05-Gal4 is functionally an LPC-Gal4 transgene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C)
evidence: Supported by temporal control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Bsh-KD eliminates Bsh expression in LPCs and newborn neurons.
source: As expected, Bsh-KD (R27G05-Gal4>UAS-Bsh-RNAi) eliminates Bsh expression in LPCs and newborn neurons (Figure 2A–F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-F demonstrating loss of Bsh expression.

claim: Bsh remains undetectable in the lamina neurons in the adult following Bsh-KD, despite the lack of RNAi expression.
source: Bsh remains undetectable in the lamina neurons in the adult, despite the lack of RNAi expression, which indicates that Bsh expression is unable to reinitiate in neurons if lost in LPCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A'–B')
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in adult flies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A'-B'.

claim: Bsh-KD resulted in a nearly complete loss of Ap and Pdm3 expression.
source: Importantly, Bsh-KD resulted in a nearly complete loss of Ap and Pdm3 expression (Figure 2G–J)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: The number of Elav+ lamina neurons is unchanged following Bsh-KD.
source: these neurons are not dying, as the number of Elav+ lamina neurons is unchanged (Figure 2K)
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2K demonstrating no change in total neuron number.

claim: Ectopic Ap expression in L5 is caused by the R27G05-Gal4 line, probably due to its genome insertion site.
source: Note that ectopic Ap expression in L5 is caused by the R27G05-Gal4 line, probably due to its genome insertion site, but this does not affect our conclusion that Bsh is required for Ap and Pdm3 expression
evidence: Based on observation of ectopic expression pattern and inference about the cause.

claim: Bsh Crispr/Cas9 knockout shows similar results to Bsh-KD.
source: Consistent with the Bsh-KD phenotype, we found similar results using a Bsh Crispr/Cas9 knockout (KO) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E–I)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-I.

claim: The primary HDTF Bsh is required to drive the expression of the secondary HDTFs Ap and Pdm3 and specify L4/L5 neuronal fates.
source: we conclude that the primary HDTF Bsh is required to drive the expression of the secondary HDTFs Ap and Pdm3 and specify L4/L5 neuronal fates (Figure 2L)
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function experiments showing loss of Ap and Pdm3 when Bsh is knocked down.

claim: Bsh is not required to maintain Ap expression in L4 neurons.
source: These results show (a) that all known lamina neuron markers are independent of Bsh regulation in neurons and (b) that Ap may undergo positive autoregulation after its initiation, rendering it independent of Bsh. Autoregulation is a common feature of HDTFs (Leyva-Díaz and Hobert, 2019). We conclude that Bsh is not required to maintain Ap expression or repress other lamina neuron markers in L4 neurons
evidence: Supported by Bsh knockout experiments in L4 neurons showing maintained Ap expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and cited literature on HDTF autoregulation.

claim: Bsh-KD led to ectopic expression of the L1 and L3 markers Svp and Erm in the positions normally occupied by L4/L5 cell bodies.
source: We found that Bsh-KD led to ectopic expression of the L1 and L3 markers Svp and Erm in the positions normally occupied by L4/L5 cell bodies (Figure 3A–E)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A-E demonstrating ectopic marker expression.

claim: Cell bodies never co-expressed Erm and Svp in Bsh-KD.
source: Notably, we never saw cell bodies co-expressing Erm and Svp, excluding the possibility of an ectopic hybrid neuronal fate in Bsh-KD
evidence: Based on observation of mutually exclusive marker expression in immunostaining data.

claim: The L2 marker Bab2 was unaffected by Bsh-KD.
source: In contrast, the L2 marker Bab2 was unaffected by Bsh-KD (Figure 3F–H)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The absence of Bsh may generate ectopic L1 and L3 neuron types at the expense of L4 and L5.
source: Together, our data suggest that the absence of Bsh may generate ectopic L1 and L3 neuron types at the expense of L4 and L5
evidence: Inferred from data showing ectopic L1/L3 markers and loss of L4/L5 markers with unchanged total neuron number.

claim: Bsh-KD generated GFP+ neurons that turn on L1 marker Svp instead of L5 marker Pdm3.
source: In contrast, Bsh-KD generated GFP+ neurons that turn on L1 marker Svp instead of L5 marker Pdm3 (Figure 3I–L)
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data using Bsh-LexA shown in Figure 3I-L.

claim: Some of the GFP+Svp+ neurons had cell bodies displaced from the L5 layer into the L1 layer following Bsh-KD.
source: Interestingly, some of the GFP+Svp+ neurons had cell bodies displaced from the L5 layer into the L1 layer (Figure 3J), which suggests that L1 neurons may actively seek out their appropriate settling layer
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3J and inference about cell migration behavior.

claim: Bsh-KD resulted in GFP+ neurons elaborating L1-like dendrite arbors – bushy dendrites throughout the lamina.
source: In contrast, Bsh-KD resulted in GFP+ neurons elaborating L1-like dendrite arbors – bushy dendrites throughout the lamina (Figure 3N and O; summarized in Figure 3P)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: Control L5 neurons have very few dendrites in the lamina neuropil.
source: In control, GFP+ neurons, which trace L5 neurons, have very few dendrites in the lamina neuropil (Figure 3M)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Bsh-KD generates L1 neuron type at the expense of L5.
source: Because Bsh-KD generates L1 neuron type at the expense of L5, the ectopic L3 neurons must be generated at the expense of L4, which is confirmed by our accompanying work (Xu et al., 2023)
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing and marker expression data, with support from cited accompanying work.

claim: Loss of Ap did not affect Bsh expression in L4.
source: Importantly, loss of Ap did not affect Bsh expression in L4 and did not lead to ectopic expression of other lamina neuron markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Bsh but not Ap is required to repress L1/L3 neuronal fates.
source: suggesting that Bsh but not Ap is required to repress L1/L3 neuronal fates
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Bsh-KD and Ap-KD phenotypes.

claim: The primary HDTF Bsh, but not the secondary HDTF Ap, promotes L4/L5 neuronal fates and suppresses L1/L3 fates, thereby generating lamina neuronal diversity.
source: we conclude that the primary HDTF Bsh, but not the secondary HDTF Ap, promotes L4/L5 neuronal fates and suppresses L1/L3 fates, thereby generating lamina neuronal diversity (Figure 3P)
evidence: Supported by comparison of Bsh-KD and Ap-KD phenotypes showing different effects on neuronal fate.

claim: The HDTF Zfh1 was present in all LPCs before becoming restricted to L1 and L3 neurons.
source: To find this HDTF, we screened published RNA-seq data (Tan et al., 2015) and found that the HDTF Zfh1 was present in all LPCs before becoming restricted to L1 and L3 neurons (Figure 4A–D)
evidence: Supported by published RNA-seq data and immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Zfh1-KD significantly decreased Zfh1 nuclear levels in all LPCs and neurons.
source: As expected, Zfh1-KD significantly decreased Zfh1 nuclear levels in all LPCs and neurons (Figure 4D–E''; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4D-E'' and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Zfh1-KD resulted in a loss of Svp+ L1 and Erm+ L3 neurons.
source: and resulted in a loss of Svp+ L1 and Erm+ L3 neurons (Figure 4D–F), consistent with a role in specifying L1 and L3 neuronal identity
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Zhf1-KD did not increase the total number of Ap/Pdm3+ neurons.
source: In contrast, Zhf1-KD did not increase the total number of Ap/Pdm3+ neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G), showing that Zfh1 does not repress L4/L5 neuronal identity
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Zfh1-KD resulted in fewer lamina neurons overall, including a reduction of Bsh+ L4 and L5 neurons.
source: We observed that Zfh1-KD resulted in fewer lamina neurons overall, including a reduction of Bsh+ L4 and L5 neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E'–K); this suggests a potential role for Zfh1 in LPCs in regulating lamina neurogenesis
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E'-K and inference about Zfh1 function.

claim: Bsh-KD resulted in ectopic expression of Zfh1 in the L4/L5 cell body layers and in GFP+ neurons (normally L5).
source: Importantly, Bsh-KD (R27G05-Gal4>Bsh-RNAi) resulted in ectopic expression of Zfh1 in the L4/L5 cell body layers and in GFP+ neurons (normally L5) (Figure 4G–I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L–N)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 4G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1L-N.

claim: Bsh and Zfh1 are both primary HDTFs (specifying L4/L5 and L1/L3, respectively).
source: We propose that Bsh and Zfh1 are both primary HDTFs (specifying L4/L5 and L1/L3, respectively) and that Bsh represses Zfh1 to suppress L1/L3 neuronal fates (Figure 4J)
evidence: Inferred from expression timing and loss-of-function data showing their roles in fate specification.

claim: Bsh represses Zfh1 to suppress L1/L3 neuronal fates.
source: We propose that Bsh and Zfh1 are both primary HDTFs (specifying L4/L5 and L1/L3, respectively) and that Bsh represses Zfh1 to suppress L1/L3 neuronal fates (Figure 4J)
evidence: Inferred from data showing ectopic Zfh1 expression when Bsh is knocked down.

claim: There are 958 genes that are significantly transcribed in L4 at 48 hr or 60 hr APF.
source: There are 958 genes that are significantly transcribed in L4 at 48 hr or 60 hr APF
evidence: Based on analysis of published scRNA-seq data from L4 neurons.

claim: Among genes transcribed in L4, 421 genes show Bsh:Dam binding peaks, while 537 genes do not show Bsh:Dam binding peaks.
source: Among them, 421 genes show Bsh:Dam binding peaks, while 537 genes do not show Bsh:Dam binding peaks (Figure 5C)
evidence: Based on integration of Bsh:Dam TaDa data with scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DIP-β is specifically expressed in L4 neurites in the proximal lamina.
source: We previously showed that DIP-β, a cell surface protein of the immunoglobulin superfamily, is specifically expressed in L4 neurites in the proximal lamina, and is required for proper L4 circuit formation (Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on previously published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: DIP-β is required for proper L4 circuit formation.
source: We previously showed that DIP-β, a cell surface protein of the immunoglobulin superfamily, is specifically expressed in L4 neurites in the proximal lamina, and is required for proper L4 circuit formation (Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on previously published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Bsh binding peaks in L4 neurons are found within the first intron of the DIP-β gene.
source: Here, we found Bsh binding peaks in L4 neurons within the first intron of the DIP-β gene (Figure 5D)
evidence: Supported by Bsh:Dam TaDa data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Ecdysone receptor (EcR) has a DNA-binding motif in the DIP-β first intron.
source: Interestingly, the Ecdysone receptor (EcR), which controls the temporal expression of DIP-β in L4 neurons, also has a DNA-binding motif in the DIP-β first intron (Jain et al., 2022)
evidence: Based on published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Bsh and the EcR pathway may cooperate to achieve the proper spatial (Bsh) and temporal (EcR) expression pattern of the DIP-β synapse recognition molecule.
source: suggesting Bsh and the EcR pathway may cooperate to achieve the proper spatial (Bsh) and temporal (EcR) expression pattern of the DIP-β synapse recognition molecule
evidence: Inferred from the presence of both Bsh and EcR binding sites in the DIP-β locus.

claim: Bsh:Dam shows direct binding to L4 identity genes as well as pan-neuronal genes.
source: Taken together, consistent with the work of terminal selector in C. elegans, we found evidence that Bsh:Dam shows direct binding to L4 identity genes – including DIP-β – as well as pan-neuronal genes (summarized in Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by Bsh:Dam TaDa data shown in Figure 5D and comparison to C. elegans terminal selector function.

claim: Bsh:Dam showed a Bsh binding peak at the ap locus.
source: We found that Bsh:Dam showed a Bsh binding peak at the ap locus, suggesting that Bsh may redundantly maintain Ap expression in L4 neurons through the stage of synapse formation (along with potential Ap-positive autoregulation) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by Bsh:Dam TaDa data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Bsh:Dam did not show binding peaks at pdm3 or zfh1 loci.
source: In contrast, Bsh:Dam did not show binding peaks at pdm3 or zfh1 loci, which might be due to the inaccessibility of pdm3 or zfh1 loci in L4 neurons
evidence: Supported by Bsh:Dam TaDa data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and inference about chromatin accessibility.

claim: Dam (open chromatin) does not show a peak at pdm3 or zfh1 loci, suggesting that pdm3 or zfh1 loci are not accessible in L4 neurons during synaptogenesis.
source: Indeed, Dam (open chromatin) (Aughey et al., 2018) does not show a peak at pdm3 or zfh1 loci, suggesting that pdm3 or zfh1 loci are not accessible in L4 neurons during synaptogenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by Dam control data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and cited literature on Dam as an open chromatin marker.

claim: Bsh-KO only in L4 neurons resulted in a strong decrease in DIP-β levels.
source: We found that Bsh-KO (31C06-AD, 34G07-DBD>UAS-Cas9, UAS-Bsh-sgRNAs) only in L4 neurons resulted in a strong decrease in DIP-β levels (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: L4 primary dendrite length and presynaptic Bruchpilot (Brp) puncta in the proximal lamina were both decreased following Bsh-KO.
source: Furthermore, using the STaR method (Chen et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2019), we found that L4 primary dendrite length and presynaptic Bruchpilot (Brp) puncta in the proximal lamina were both decreased following Bsh-KO (Figure 6E–I)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and synapse quantification shown in Figure 6E-I, using methods from cited literature.

claim: Bsh-KO has a distinct phenotype from DIP-β-KD.
source: this is distinct from the DIP-β-KD phenotype (Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on comparison with previously published DIP-β-KD phenotype.

claim: Bsh is required to activate DIP-β expression in L4 and regulate L4 morphology and connectivity.
source: We conclude that Bsh is required to activate DIP-β expression in L4 and regulate L4 morphology and connectivity
evidence: Inferred from Bsh-KO experiments showing loss of DIP-β and altered L4 morphology/connectivity.

claim: Bsh likely has distinct targets in addition to DIP-β.
source: Because Bsh-KO has a distinct phenotype from DIP-β-KD, it is likely that Bsh has distinct targets in addition to DIP-β
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Bsh-KO and DIP-β-KD phenotypes showing non-identical effects.

claim: Ap-KD in L4 neurons resulted in a strong decrease in DIP-β levels.
source: To test whether Ap controls DIP-β expression in L4, we knocked down Ap in L4 neurons (R27G05-Gal4>Ap-RNAi) and observed a strong decrease in DIP-β levels in L4 neurons (Figure 6J–M)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6J-M.

claim: Ap-KD in L4 neurons increased Brp puncta in the distal/proximal lamina and increased the length of L4 primary dendrites.
source: Importantly, Ap-KD in L4 neurons increased Brp puncta in the distal/proximal lamina and increased the length of L4 primary dendrites, which is similar to DIP-β-KD phenotype (Xu et al., 2019; Figure 6N–R)
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis and synapse quantification shown in Figure 6N-R, with comparison to cited literature.

claim: Ap is required to activate DIP-β expression in L4 and regulate L4 morphology and connectivity mainly through DIP-β.
source: We conclude that Ap is required to activate DIP-β expression in L4 and regulate L4 morphology and connectivity mainly through DIP-β
evidence: Inferred from Ap-KD experiments showing loss of DIP-β and phenotype similar to DIP-β-KD.

claim: A coherent feed-forward motif is A activates B, followed by A and B, both activating C.
source: A coherent feed-forward motif is A activates B, followed by A and B, both activating C (Mangan and Alon, 2003)
evidence: Based on established definition from cited literature.

claim: Bsh activates Ap in L4 neurons soon after their birth.
source: Bsh activates Ap in L4 neurons soon after their birth (Figure 2G and H)
evidence: Supported by temporal expression data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Bsh and Ap are both required to activate DIP-β.
source: and Bsh and Ap are both required to activate DIP-β (Figure 6A–D and J–M)
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function experiments shown in Figure 6A-D and J-M.

claim: Loss of Bsh in L4 neurons decreases DIP-β levels without altering Ap expression.
source: Importantly, loss of Bsh in L4 neurons decreases DIP-β levels (Figure 6A–D) without altering Ap expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 4F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Bsh activates Ap, and then both are independently required to promote expression of the synapse recognition gene DIP-β, thereby bridging neuronal fate decision to synaptic connectivity.
source: In conclusion, we have defined a coherent feed-forward loop in which Bsh activates Ap, and then both are independently required to promote expression of the synapse recognition gene DIP-β, thereby bridging neuronal fate decision to synaptic connectivity (Figure 6)
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing Bsh activates Ap, and both independently regulate DIP-β.

claim: Bsh-KD in LPCs resulted in a lack of Bsh in the adult lamina.
source: We found that Bsh-KD in LPCs resulted in a lack of Bsh in the adult lamina (Isaacson et al., 2023; Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and cited work.

claim: Flies with Bsh-KD in LPCs, where L4/L5 neurons are transformed into L1/L3 neurons, showed a reduced response to a high-speed stimulus.
source: Flies with Bsh-KD in LPCs, where L4/L5 neurons are transformed into L1/L3 neurons, showed a reduced response to a high-speed stimulus, suggesting weakened sensitivity to visual motion (Figure 7B)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Fly Vision Box experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: L4 function is not required for motion detection when silencing L4 or L5 neuron activity alone.
source: Previous work found that L4 function is not required for motion detection when silencing L4 or L5 neuron activity alone (Silies et al., 2013; Tuthill et al., 2013)
evidence: Based on previously published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: L4 and L5 acting together might be required for normal sensitivity to visual motion.
source: which suggests that L4 and L5 acting together might be required for normal sensitivity to visual motion
evidence: Inferred from comparison of current results with cited literature showing individual L4 or L5 silencing has no effect.

claim: Bsh-KD flies had reduced phototaxis to both dim and bright lights when tested with both UV and green LEDs.
source: When tested with both UV and green LEDs, the Bsh-KD flies had reduced phototaxis to both dim and bright lights, suggesting less sensitivity to both UV and green lights
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Fly Vision Box experiments shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Bsh-KD flies exhibited larger responses toward bright UV illumination in the spectral preference assay.
source: Interestingly, the Bsh-KD flies exhibited larger responses toward bright UV illumination in the spectral preference assay (Figure 7C and D)
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Fly Vision Box experiments shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The apparent attraction to bright UV light in Bsh-KD flies may result from more weakened sensitivity to green light.
source: This apparent attraction to bright UV light may result from more weakened sensitivity to green light, which may be expected since L4 and L5 are indirect R1-6 targets (Takemura et al., 2015)
evidence: Inferred from behavioral data and cited literature on L4/L5 connectivity.

claim: The primary HDTF Bsh is required to generate lamina neuronal diversity and normal visual behavior.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the primary HDTF Bsh is required to generate lamina neuronal diversity and normal visual behavior (Figure 7E)
evidence: Supported by combined data showing Bsh-KD reduces neuronal diversity and impairs visual behavior.

claim: HDTFs function hierarchically in coupling neuronal fate specification to circuit assembly.
source: Here, we show that HDTFs function hierarchically in coupling neuronal fate specification to circuit assembly
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing primary HDTF Bsh activates secondary HDTFs and regulates circuit formation.

claim: In L4 neurons, Bsh and Ap function in a feed-forward loop to activate the synapse recognition molecule DIP-β, thereby bridging neuronal fate decision to synaptic connectivity.
source: Third, in L4 neurons, Bsh and Ap function in a feed-forward loop to activate the synapse recognition molecule (DIP-β), thereby bridging neuronal fate decision to synaptic connectivity
evidence: Supported by data showing both Bsh and Ap independently regulate DIP-β expression and connectivity.

claim: Hierarchical HDTFs may represent a conserved mechanism for linking neuronal diversity to circuit assembly and function.
source: Hierarchical HDTFs may represent a conserved mechanism for linking neuronal diversity to circuit assembly and function
evidence: Speculated based on findings in Drosophila and comparison to C. elegans terminal selector mechanisms.

claim: In both Drosophila and mouse, spatial and temporal factors act combinatorially to generate molecularly distinct newborn neurons.
source: in both Drosophila and mouse, spatial and temporal factors act combinatorially to generate molecularly distinct newborn neurons (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013; Doe, 2017; Erclik et al., 2017; Holguera and Desplan, 2018; Sen et al., 2019)
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple cited references.

claim: Most spatial and temporal factors are only transiently present in newborn neurons.
source: Yet, most spatial and temporal factors are only transiently present in newborn neurons
evidence: Based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Each adult neuron type in C. elegans expresses a unique combination of homeodomain TFs, which have been called terminal selectors.
source: Work from the Hobert lab in Caenorhabditis elegans found that each adult neuron type expresses a unique combination of homeodomain TFs (HDTFs), which have been called terminal selectors (Hobert, 2021; Reilly et al., 2020)
evidence: Based on published work from the Hobert lab cited in the manuscript.

claim: Terminal selector HDTFs drive the expression of neuron functional identity genes and activate pan-neuronal genes.
source: Terminal selector HDTFs not only drive the expression of neuron functional identity genes but also activate pan-neuronal genes (Hobert, 2021; Howell et al., 2015; Kratsios et al., 2015; Stefanakis et al., 2015)
evidence: Based on published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of terminal selector HDTFs frequently results in altered neuronal identity and function.
source: Loss of terminal selector HDTFs frequently results in altered neuronal identity and function (Arlotta and Hobert, 2015; Cros and Hobert, 2022; Reilly et al., 2022)
evidence: Based on published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila lamina has only five intrinsic neuron types (L1-L5), which are analogous to bipolar cells in the vertebrate.
source: The Drosophila lamina has only five intrinsic neuron types (L1-L5), which are analogous to bipolar cells in the vertebrate (Sanes and Zipursky, 2010)
evidence: Based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: During late larval and early pupal stages, lamina progenitor cells (LPCs) give rise to L1-L5 neurons.
source: During late larval and early pupal stages, lamina progenitor cells (LPCs) give rise to L1-L5 neurons (Fernandes et al., 2017; Huang et al., 1998)
evidence: Based on published work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The core motion detection neurons L1-L3 receive direct synaptic inputs from photoreceptors and mediate visual motion detection.
